title: Rhodes
capsule: Rhodes was a powerful Greek city-state on the island of the same name at the southwestern tip of the Aegean, famous for its navy, its Colossus (erected c. 280 BCE), and its role as the Mediterranean's preeminent commercial and juridical maritime power from the 3rd century BCE. After aiding Rome against the Seleucids, Rhodes was rewarded by the Treaty of Apamea (188 BCE) with extensive Anatolian territory, marking the high point of its independent influence. Relations with Rome deteriorated during the Third Macedonian War (171–168 BCE), when Rhodes's neutrality was perceived as pro-Macedonian sympathy; Rome punished it by establishing a free port at Delos, devastating Rhodian commercial revenues. By 164 BCE Rhodes had concluded a permanent alliance with Rome, becoming effectively a client state, though it retained nominal independence and continued as a celebrated center of rhetoric and philosophy for Roman aristocrats.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The island's boundaries are geographically fixed; its continental possessions in Lycia and Caria after 188 BCE are documented in ancient sources but their precise limits fluctuated with political circumstances.
